title: Metrics & Dashboards
description: Master metrics collection with Prometheus, understand counters, gauges, and histograms, and learn why percentiles matter more than averages.

segments.text: Logs tell you what happened. Metrics tell you how your system is performing right now. Today we'll learn how to collect, aggregate, and visualize metrics — the numbers that keep your system alive at three in the morning.

Prometheus is the industry standard for metrics. It works on a pull model: Prometheus periodically scrapes HTTP endpoints from your services. Each service exposes its metrics at a /metrics endpoint. No agents to install, no push infrastructure to manage.

A counter is a metric that only goes up. Total HTTP requests served, total errors, total bytes sent. You never reset a counter — Prometheus calculates the rate of change for you. Rate of requests per second is just the derivative of the counter.

A gauge can go up or down. Current CPU usage, memory consumption, number of active connections, queue depth. Gauges capture the current value of something, like a speedometer. They're sampled at scrape time.

Histograms are the most powerful metric type. They bucket observations into ranges. For request latency, you might have buckets at 10ms, 50ms, 100ms, 500ms, and 1 second. This lets you calculate percentiles, which are far more useful than averages.
segments.thought_prompt: Why is 'average latency is 100ms' misleading? What could it be hiding?

segments.text: Average latency can lie. If 99 requests take 10ms and one takes 10 seconds, the average is 109ms — which describes nobody's experience. The p50 is 10ms, the p99 is 10 seconds. Percentiles show the distribution, not just the center.

P50 is your median — half of requests are faster. P95 means 95 percent of requests are faster. P99 means only 1 in 100 is slower. At scale, that 1 percent affects millions of users. Google and Amazon obsess over p99 because it directly impacts revenue.

Grafana is the visualization layer. It connects to Prometheus and lets you build dashboards with graphs, gauges, and alerts. A good dashboard answers three questions at a glance: is the system healthy, how is it performing, and where are the bottlenecks?

Two frameworks help you decide what to measure. RED for services: Rate, Errors, Duration. USE for resources: Utilization, Saturation, Errors. RED tells you if your service is healthy. USE tells you if your infrastructure is healthy.
segments.thought_prompt: Which RED or USE metric would you check first during an outage?

segments.text: Metrics power your alerts. Alert on symptoms, not causes. Don't alert when CPU is high — alert when error rate exceeds one percent or p99 latency exceeds 500ms. High CPU might be normal during a traffic spike. High error rate is always a problem.

Counters for totals, gauges for current values, histograms for distributions. Percentiles over averages. RED and USE as your measurement frameworks. And always alert on symptoms. These are the fundamentals of metrics-based observability. Next: distributed tracing.
